title: Joystick Control and Vessel Handling
description: The TDPO learns to control vessel motion with precision, efficiency and professional discipline in any environmental condition. Professional standard means minimum inputs, no overcorrections, deliberate deceleration planned before it is needed, vessel arrives at intended position with near-zero residual velocity.

tasks.title: Pure Drift Stop
tasks.setup: Note your exact current position on the motion page. This is your datum. You will not be returning to it in this task — the only goal is stopping.
tasks.execute: Select JSMH and set all joystick inputs to zero. Let the vessel drift freely for exactly 4 minutes. Do not touch any controls. When 4 minutes expires, using joystick only, bring the vessel to a complete stop. Both velocity axes must read below 0.1kts. Do not return to datum — stopping is the entire task.
professional_standard: Stopped within 3 deliberate joystick inputs
Residual velocity below 0.1kts on both axes
Heading maintained throughout — no yaw during the stop
No overcorrection after initial input

fields.label: Time from first input to stop (seconds)

debrief_questions: Which direction did the vessel drift and which environmental force dominated — wind, wave or current? How do you know?

At the speed your vessel was moving when you intervened, and knowing your stopping distance — at what range from a hard exclusion zone would you have needed to begin your deceleration to stop cleanly?
Why does stopping a vessel into the weather require different technique to stopping beam-on to it?
If wind increased from 15kts to 25kts mid-stop, what would change about your technique and why?

The DP mathematical model builds its understanding of environmental forces partly from thruster activity. After a large joystick transit, what does the model incorrectly learn — and why does selecting Monitor briefly before DP help the model reset more accurately than going straight from JSMH to DP?

variants.title: Extended Drift Stop
variants.note_to_tdpo: More speed to manage. Start your deceleration earlier than you think you need to.

variants.title: Beam Drift Stop
variants.note_to_tdpo: The vessel will behave completely differently. Tunnel thruster geometry means beam stopping authority differs from head/stern stopping authority. Notice which thrusters the system uses.

variants.title: Drift Stop with Position Constraint
variants.note_to_tdpo: Now you have two objectives. Stopping cleanly AND where you stop matters. This begins introducing position awareness into speed management.

variants.title: Drift, Stop and Return
variants.note_to_tdpo: This is the complete manoeuvre. Three distinct phases. Do not start the return until velocity is below 0.1kts. Do not engage DP until you are within the DP operating radius and below 0.1kts.

tasks.title: Controlled Surge Move
tasks.setup: Confirm your exact datum position. You will return to within 2m of this position at the end of each run.
tasks.execute: Move the vessel exactly 100m North from datum. Stop with residual velocity below 0.1kts. Return to within 2m of original datum position. This is one run. Complete three runs.
professional_standard: Overshoot less than 5m on return each run
Residual velocity below 0.1kts at stop each run
Improvement visible between run 1 and run 3
Heading maintained throughout

fields_per_run.label: Return accuracy — distance from exact datum (metres)

debrief_questions: Did your overshoot reduce between run 1 and run 3? What specifically changed in your technique?
At what point in each run did you decide to begin decelerating — and in hindsight was that the right point?
Why is a 100m surge move (North/South) typically easier to execute cleanly than a 100m sway move (East/West) on most DP vessels? Think about thruster geometry.
In a real operation near a rig, what would be the consequence of a 5m overshoot versus a 15m overshoot?

variants.title: Short Surge Move
variants.note_to_tdpo: Shorter distance, less time to manage deceleration. Harder than it sounds.

variants.title: Long Surge Move
variants.note_to_tdpo: More speed builds, earlier deceleration decision required.

variants.title: Surge Move in Wind
variants.note_to_tdpo: Same task, different feel. Apply all three runs in the same wind condition.

variants.title: Controlled Sway Move
variants.note_to_tdpo: Direct comparison of surge vs sway handling. Same distance, same standard. Notice what is different.

tasks.title: Controlled Sway Move
tasks.setup: Confirm exact datum position. You will return to within 2m of this position at the end of each run.
tasks.execute: Move the vessel exactly 100m East from datum. Stop with residual velocity below 0.1kts. Return to within 2m of original datum. This is one run. Complete three runs. Compare your results to jc_002.
professional_standard: Overshoot less than 5m on return each run
Residual velocity below 0.1kts at stop each run
Improvement visible between run 1 and run 3
Heading maintained throughout
debrief_questions: Was the sway move harder or easier than the surge move in jc_002? What specifically explains the difference?
Which thrusters did the most work during the sway move — and why those ones based on their position on the vessel?
What does this tell you about the vessel's athwartship stopping authority compared to fore-aft?
In a real operation, when would you need to make a pure sway move rather than repositioning on DP?

variants.title: Short Sway Move
variants.note_to_tdpo: Shorter distance — less time to manage deceleration. Harder than it sounds in the athwartship axis.

variants.title: Sway Move in Wind
variants.note_to_tdpo: Same task in wind. Notice how beam-on wind affects sway control differently to how head wind affected surge control.

tasks.title: Diagonal Move
tasks.setup: Confirm datum. Calm conditions only for first run.
tasks.execute: Move the vessel 100m Northeast simultaneously — not North then East in sequence, but both axes at the same time. Stop with residual below 0.1kts on both axes. Return to datum. Three runs.
professional_standard: Heading maintained within 3 degrees throughout
Both axes within 5m overshoot on return
Residual velocity below 0.1kts at stop
Smooth coordinated inputs — no axis fighting

fields_per_run.label: Which axis was harder to control?

debrief_questions: Which axis was harder to control simultaneously and what caused the difficulty?
Did your heading drift during the move — what caused it and how did you correct?
In what real operational scenario would a diagonal move be required rather than sequential axis moves?
How does the DP thrust allocation algorithm handle simultaneous surge and sway demand — does it prioritise one axis?

variants.title: Diagonal Move in Moderate Conditions
variants.note_to_tdpo: Same task with wind. The wind vector intersects your movement vector — notice how this changes which axis is harder.

tasks.title: Heading Change at Controlled Rate
tasks.setup: Note current heading. This is your start heading. Your target is current heading plus 45 degrees.
tasks.execute: Change vessel heading by 45 degrees at no more than 2 degrees per minute. Stop exactly on the new heading. Record position excursion during the turn. Then return to original heading at 5 degrees per minute. Record excursion on return.
professional_standard: Rate of turn does not exceed 2 degrees per minute on slow turn
Position excursion under 5m during turn
Stop within 1 degree of target heading
Heading maintained on return

fields.label: Maximum position excursion during slow turn (metres)
Heading accuracy at stop — degrees off target
Maximum position excursion during fast return (metres)

debrief_questions: Why did position keeping degrade during the heading change even though you were on DP auto position?
Why would you limit rate of turn to 2 degrees per minute near a structure?
What happens to thruster allocation geometry as the vessel rotates — which thrusters change role?
When would you use a fast heading change versus a slow controlled turn operationally?

variants.title: 90 Degree Heading Change
variants.note_to_tdpo: Larger rotation means longer period of degraded position keeping. Plan for more excursion and debrief on where the worst excursion occurred in the turn.

variants.title: Heading Change Near Structure
variants.note_to_tdpo: Same turn but with a virtual structure 150m away. Your excursion margin is now constrained. Does your technique change?

tasks.title: Emergency Stop from Speed
tasks.setup: Moderate conditions set. Vessel on DP at datum. Identify a clear stopping lane with no constraints.
tasks.execute: Deliberately build the vessel to 1.0kt forward speed using joystick. Then stop as quickly and cleanly as possible. Record stopping distance. Reset to datum. Repeat three times — try to improve stopping distance each run.
professional_standard: Stop within 30m from 1.0kt in moderate conditions
Residual velocity below 0.1kts at stop
No heading change greater than 5 degrees during stop
Improvement between run 1 and run 3
debrief_questions: What was your stopping distance from 1.0kt? Is that a safe margin at 100m from a hard exclusion zone?
What specific technique change reduced your stopping distance between runs?
How does heading relative to wind affect stopping efficiency — is it easier to stop into the weather or with it?
At what speed would you consider the vessel out of safe control in a DP operational context near structure?

variants.title: Emergency Stop from Higher Speed
variants.note_to_tdpo: Faster entry speed. Stopping distance will increase non-linearly. Notice how much earlier you need to intervene.

variants.title: Emergency Stop in Heavy Weather
variants.note_to_tdpo: Heavy conditions change everything about stopping. Environmental forces may assist or resist depending on your heading. Assess before you act.

tasks.title: Blind Stop Challenge
tasks.environment: Set by DPO — unknown to trainee
tasks.setup: DPO sets a random drift duration between 3 and 8 minutes and an environment the trainee has not seen. Trainee does not know duration or conditions in advance.
tasks.execute: DPO starts the drift without telling the trainee how long it will run. Trainee observes the drift. When DPO gives the instruction to stop — stop the vessel. No preparation time. Residual velocity and time to stop are your score.
professional_standard: Residual velocity below 0.2kts
Vessel stopped within 60 seconds of instruction
Correct assessment of dominant environmental force stated before acting
Heading maintained during stop

fields.label: Dominant force assessed — wind, wave or current?

debrief_questions: How did unknown conditions change your approach compared to prepared drills?
What information did you gather in the first 30 seconds of observation — and was it enough?
How does this drill simulate real operational conditions when DP fails unexpectedly?
What is the difference in your mental process between a prepared stop and a blind stop?

variants.title: Blind Stop with Position Constraint
variants.note_to_tdpo: Same blind stop but a virtual structure is active. You must stop before reaching the alert zone. Stakes are now real.
